title: Step-by-Step Guide to Building Permit Acquisition
summary: Navigate the permit acquisition process step by step. Plus, learn how to pull permits faster with permitting software like PermitFlow.
body_text: The process of pulling a building permit can make or break your project’s timeline. Navigating jurisdictional requirements, documentation review standards, and review cycles is complex and time-consuming, especially when you’re balancing multiple projects at the same time. This guide covers each step of the permit acquisition process, with insights on how you can streamline the approval process and keep your projects moving efficiently. Step 1: Determine whether or not a permit is required Not all projects require a building permit, but many do. Most structural modifications, such as framing, roofing, HVAC installation , plumbing , electrical work , and demolition will all require permits depending on your local jurisdiction. More speciality installations, such as EV charging equipment , backup generators , or other mechanical upgrades also typically call for separate or additional permits. The requirements for each permit vary across both commercial and residential projects. Commercial projects often require more detail due to safety standards, occupancy requirements, and multi-phase inspections because of the complexity of the project. Residential permits are often easier to acquire, but will still be subjected to local building codes. ‍ Step 2: Understand local jurisdiction requirements Every jurisdiction has its own permitting rules, documentation standards, submittal processes , inspection scheduling procedures, approval timelines, and more. City, county, or state-level regulations may dictate design requirements, energy efficiency standards, environmental restrictions, and zoning approvals. Researching permit requirements can become time-consuming, especially if you’re managing projects across multiple regions. AHJ’s requirements are often unclear, and their websites might be outdated. Using a permit management tool like PermitFlow can provide jurisdiction-specific guidelines and save you the hassle of researching requirements yourself. ‍ Step 3: Gather required documentation Gathering the correct documentation for your permit is often the most time-consuming and error-prone part of the permit acquisition process. The most common required documentation includes: Construction drawings and site plans Engineering calculations or load reports Energy model or solar panel layout diagrams Project scope description Contractor licenses and insurance certifications Product specifications (e.g., energy storage, EV equipment) Fire safety or environmental impact assessments Commercial projects will require stamped drawings from licensed engineers, while residential projects often accept standard building plans. Ensure formats, scale requirements, and digital file types all meet the requirements set by your jurisdiction. Pro tip: Use permitting software like PermitFlow to generate project-specific document checklists, keep files organized in the cloud, and manage version control. It’ll help your team stay aligned, prevent missing documents, and reduce avoidable review delays. ‍ Step 4: Prepare the permit application Once you have all of your documents ready, you will need to prepare the full application. This usually requires entering project information, specifying the scope of work, listing subcontractors, and detailing estimated project costs or square footage. Some jurisdictions require digital submissions via online permitting portals, while others require in-person paper applications. Common permit application mistakes include: Incomplete project descriptions Incorrect valuation figures Submitting outdated forms Review your application before submission to avoid review delays or rejection. ‍ Step 5: Submit the permit and pay fees You’ll have to submit your application online, by mail, or in person depending on your jurisdiction’s rules. Fee structures vary greatly depending on your jurisdiction. Some municipalities calculate permit fees based on project valuation; others on square footage, service type, or specialty use. Additional fees may be required for engineering reviews, zoning clearances, or expedited service. Tracking fees is an important part of managing your project, especially when you’re managing several permits across multiple projects. Some advanced software integrates with digital submission platforms and enables electronic payment tracking. Some systems provide real-time updates if fees change due to rule updates or application modifications. ‍ Step 6: Respond and reply to review comments Once your application is submitted, your project undergoes plan review. This can involve various departments, such as building, fire, planning, electrical, environmental, and in some cases, utility providers. Reviewers may request clarifications or revisions before granting final approval. Addressing comments promptly will help prevent delays. Having a designated internal process for assigning revision tasks to other stakeholders — like architects, engineers, or subcontractors — can greatly improve your team’s turnaround time. In this situation, permit management software helps by: Centralizing revision requests Tracking task assignments Sending automated reminders to responsible team members ‍ Step 7: Receive approval and schedule inspections Once your application is approved, your permit is issued either digitally or in a physical form. Approval timelines vary from a few days to several weeks or months depending on the scope of the project and the AHJ’s backlog. During the construction process, inspections are typically required at important milestones such as foundation, framing, electrical rough-in, panel installation, solar interconnection, and final walkthrough. Failing to schedule inspections promptly may cause delays to your projects. Permit inspection management tools like PermitFlow allow you to log inspection milestones, schedule appointments with inspectors, and receive alerts to ensure field teams are ready to go on inspection day. ‍ Step 8: Maintain permit compliance during construction After your permit is approved, maintaining compliance means following approved plans and ensuring that any design or material changes go through the correct permit revision process. If a project extends beyond the original scope or timeline, you may need to request an extension or permit amendment. Commercial projects often require additional compliance documentation as it relates to safety, ADA accessibility, or emergency systems. Residential projects may be simpler but still must align with inspection requirements. ‍ Step 9: Close out the permit and retain documentation Final inspections are required to close out most permits. Once a permit is finalized, approved documents should be archived for future reference, insurance claims, liability protection, or resale requirements. All builders and installers involved in multi-site projects benefit from having a digital record readily accessible. ‍ Take control of your permit acquisition workflow Permit acquisition is a multi-step process that requires careful planning, detailed documentation, and ongoing compliance throughout the construction process. From an initial scope evaluation to a final inspection closeout, successfully navigating permit requirements minimizes project delays and ensures regulatory compliance. If you want an easier way to keep permits moving, PermitFlow takes the busywork off your plate. Our AI-powered permit management platform: Helps you stay organized Builds accurate submissions for any jurisdiction Keeps track of every submission without digging through emails or spreadsheets The result is a smoother process with fewer surprises. PermitFlow users see 2.5x faster permit approvals and a 90% reduction in their permitting workload. Get a demo of PermitFlow today .

title: Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution: Rethinking AI for Real Impact
summary: In a SAP x Google Cloud conversation, Casey West and Laura Marwood discuss how to get real value out of AI. Read to learn more.
body_text: There is a lot of noise around AI right now. New tools, new models, new promises. Much of the conversation is focused on speed: how AI can help us write faster, code faster, produce faster. That matters, of course. But in a recent conversation with Casey West , lead developer advocate at Google Cloud, we explored a more interesting question: what if the real value of AI is not only that it helps us move faster, but that it helps us think better? West made a point that stayed with me. Using AI simply to generate more output is only the beginning. The more powerful use case is to treat AI as a collaborator in the thinking process: something that can challenge assumptions, ask questions we might not have asked, and help us see a problem from a different angle. In that role, AI is not replacing judgment, it is creating useful friction around it. That shift matters because the work of building technology is changing. Developers are no longer just writing deterministic logic and controlling every outcome in advance. Increasingly, they are working with systems that are creative, probabilistic, and less predictable by design. That opens up huge possibilities, but it also raises the bar. Quality, guardrails, metrics, and trust become even more important when software starts to reason in ways that are not always fully scripted. The advice West offered to developers was simple and probably more durable than any specific tool or framework: fall in love with the problem, not the solution . The technologies will change. The models will change. The implementations will change. But the ability to understand a problem deeply, stay curious, and apply AI with judgment will remain valuable. Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution Click the button below to load the content from YouTube. Always allow YouTube At a time when so much of the conversation around AI feels breathless, that feels like a good way to approach this moment: not with blind enthusiasm, and not with fear, but with curiosity and discipline. What are we trying to understand? What are we trying to improve? Where would better questions, better feedback, or better judgment make the biggest difference? That is where AI starts to feel less like a wave we have to chase, and more like a capability we can shape with purpose. AI gives us new ways to build, learn, and decide. The question is not just how much more we can produce with it, but how much better our thinking can become when we use it well. title: Real-Time Insurance Verification: Save $711M in 2026
summary: 71% of dental billing pros say insurance verification is their #1 challenge. Learn how real-time automated verification cuts denials, slashes A/R days, and saves thousands monthly.
body_text: Why Real-Time Insurance Verification Is Dental's Biggest Revenue Problem in 2026 If you asked 160 dental billing professionals to name their single biggest operational headache, you might expect claim denials or staffing shortages to top the list. The actual answer is more surprising — and more actionable. According to 2026 Dental RCM Trends data from Zentist , 71% of dental revenue cycle professionals identified real-time insurance verification as their primary daily operational challenge — ranking it above claim denials, collections, and staffing combined. That's not a minor inconvenience. That's a systemic revenue leak hiding in plain sight at the front desk of most dental practices. The good news? It's also one of the most solvable problems in modern dental operations — if you're willing to stop treating it as a manual task and start treating it as a system problem. This article breaks down exactly what's broken with traditional verification workflows, what the data says about automated alternatives, and how high-performing practices in 2026 are using real-time verification to protect revenue, reduce denials, and free their teams to focus on patient care. The True Cost of Manual Insurance Verification Before we talk solutions, it's worth understanding the full scope of what manual verification actually costs your practice — because most practice owners dramatically underestimate it. Time: The Hidden Tax on Your Front Desk Manual insurance verification typically takes 10 to 15 minutes per patient when done correctly — calling the payer, navigating the IVR system, waiting on hold, and transcribing the benefits information into your practice management system. For a practice seeing 30 patients per day, that's potentially 7.5 hours of front desk time consumed by a single administrative task. According to My Billing Provider's 2026 analysis , automated real-time verification reduces that 10–15 minute process to under 5 seconds . That's not a marginal improvement — it's a complete transformation of how your front office operates. Money: The Per-Verification Cost You're Ignoring Beyond time, there's a direct dollar cost to every manual verification your team performs. Prosper AI's Real-Time Insurance Eligibility Verification Guide puts the savings from automation at over $4.12 per verification in direct cost reduction , plus more than 20 minutes of processing time saved per check. Multiply that across a practice doing 600 verifications per month, and you're looking at over $2,400 in monthly savings from this single workflow change — before you even account for the downstream impact on claim denials and rework. Accuracy: Why Human Error Is Costing You Claims Manual verification isn't just slow — it's inaccurate. Prosper AI's data shows that AI-powered verification systems achieve up to 96% accuracy , compared to just 70–80% for manual checks. That 16–26 percentage point accuracy gap translates directly into denied claims, delayed payments, and frustrated patients who thought their treatment was covered. The Revenue Cycle Domino Effect: Why Verification Is Step One Insurance verification isn't just an administrative checkbox — it's the foundation on which your entire revenue cycle is built. "Insurance verification is the 'first domino' in the revenue cycle. If it falls correctly, the rest of the process — coding, billing, and payment posting — follows seamlessly. If it fails, the entire system collapses into a cycle of denials and rework." — My Billing Provider, 2026 How Verification Errors Cascade Into Denials When eligibility information is wrong at the point of scheduling, the error doesn't surface until after the appointment — sometimes weeks later, when a claim comes back denied. By that point, your team has to: Pull the original claim and identify the eligibility error Re-verify the patient's coverage retroactively Recode and resubmit the claim Potentially write off the balance if the appeal window has closed This rework cycle is expensive, demoralizing, and entirely preventable. Zentist's 2026 survey found that 78% of dental practices report an increase in claim denials or payer scrutiny over the past year , driven by shifting payer interpretations of medical necessity and frequency limitations. In that environment, starting the revenue cycle with inaccurate eligibility data is a compounding liability. The A/R Impact: Days Matter One of the clearest metrics for measuring the downstream impact of verification quality is Days in Accounts Receivable (A/R). My Billing Provider's 2026 benchmarks show that automated real-time verification reduces average Days in A/R from 45+ days to under 25 days — cutting the revenue cycle nearly in half. For a practice collecting $100,000 per month in insurance revenue, reducing Days in A/R from 45 to 25 days means getting paid roughly $67,000 faster each month. That's not a rounding error — it's working capital that can fund equipment, staffing, or marketing. What Real-Time Verification Actually Looks Like in 2026 The term "real-time verification" gets used loosely, so it's worth being precise about what best-in-class systems actually do — and how they differ from the patchwork solutions many practices are still using. The 270/271 Transaction Standard At the technical foundation, insurance eligibility verification in the U.S. runs on the HIPAA-mandated 270/271 transaction standard — a structured electronic query (270) sent to a payer and the structured response (271) returned with the patient's eligibility and benefits information. Honey Health's 2026 breakdown of leading verification platforms explains that Availity serves as the foundational network rail over which most eligibility verification traffic travels in the U.S., connecting payers, providers, and health-IT vendors for both batch and real-time 270/271 transactions. Most major clearinghouses connect to 900–1,000 payers for eligibility queries, covering virtually all commercial insurance, Medicare, and Medicaid plans. The important caveat: Availity and similar networks are connectivity layers, not deep-verification engines. The quality of the 271 response depends entirely on what the payer chooses to include — which is why layering AI-powered interpretation on top of the raw transaction data is what separates modern verification platforms from legacy clearinghouse connections. The Dual-Query Best Practice One of the most important operational insights from 2026 implementation data is that a single eligibility check is not enough. US Tech Automations' step-by-step guide identifies the dual-query approach as the current best practice: Query 1: A real-time eligibility check at the moment of scheduling — catches immediate eligibility issues, inactive coverage, or wrong insurance information before the appointment is even booked Query 2: A batch re-query 48 hours before the appointment — catches coverage terminations, deductible resets, mid-year plan changes, or employer group changes that occurred after the initial booking Relying on a single check — even a real-time one at scheduling — leaves a gap that causes preventable denials. Patients lose coverage, change jobs, or hit annual maximums between the time they schedule and the time they sit in your chair. The 48-hour re-query closes that gap systematically. Handling Exceptions: When Automation Flags for Human Review Even the best automated systems encounter cases that require human judgment — smaller regional payers, workers' compensation plans, or certain Medicaid managed care arrangements that fall outside standard clearinghouse coverage. US Tech Automations notes that these edge cases still require supplemental manual verification. The key is designing your workflow so that automation handles the routine 85–90% of cases autonomously , while flagging the exceptions for human review with enough lead time to resolve them before the appointment. This is fundamentally different from a manual-first workflow where every verification requires human effort regardless of complexity. The Business Case: $711 Million in Industry-Wide Savings The financial case for automated real-time verification isn't just compelling at the practice level — it's staggering at the industry level. The $711 Million Opportunity A 2026 analysis published on LinkedIn by Doctible projects that the dental industry could save $711+ million in 2026 through automated electronic insurance verification — extrapolated from the ADA-reported $580 million baseline in 2023 at a 7% annual growth rate. Even if you discount that projection conservatively, the macro financial case for automation is overwhelming. Practice-Level ROI: The Numbers That Matter to You At the individual practice level, the ROI metrics from automation are equally compelling: Verification time: 10–15 minutes → under 5 seconds per patient First-pass claim acceptance rate: 70–78% (manual) → 94–96% (automated), per My Billing Provider Front desk hours saved: 10 to 20 hours per week, according to PatientXpress's 2026 analysis Days in A/R: 45+ days → under 25 days Cost per verification: Reduced by $4.12+, per Prosper AI For a practice doing 500 verifications per month, the direct cost savings alone exceed $2,000 monthly — before accounting for the value of recovered denials, reduced rework, and staff time redirected to higher-value activities. The Patient Experience Dividend There's a competitive dimension to real-time verification that often gets overlooked in the ROI conversation: patient trust and retention . Prosper AI's research found that 75% of patients say that knowing their out-of-pocket costs beforehand influences their choice of provider . When your practice can tell a patient — at the time of scheduling — exactly what their insurance covers and what they'll owe, you're not just being operationally efficient. You're differentiating yourself from every competitor who still says "we'll figure out your benefits before your appointment." Cost transparency at the point of scheduling also reduces no-shows (patients who don't understand their financial responsibility are more likely to cancel) and improves case acceptance (patients who know their coverage are more likely to proceed with recommended treatment). From Manual Task to System Problem: The Mindset Shift That Changes Everything The practices that have genuinely solved the insurance verification problem in 2026 share a common operational philosophy — and it's not about finding faster ways to do manual verification. "The practices that have solved the eligibility verification problem share one thing in common. They stopped treating it as a manual task and started treating it as a system problem. The right software doesn't just speed up what your team was already doing. It removes them from the loop entirely for the routine cases and flags the exceptions that need human attention." — Foji.io, 2026 The Adoption Gap: Where Most Practices Still Stand Despite the compelling ROI data, Foji.io's 2026 research shows that only 58% of dental practices are actively adopting automation tools for eligibility verification as of 2026. That means roughly 4 in 10 practices are still relying primarily on manual processes — absorbing the time costs, accuracy costs, and denial costs that come with them. The gap between adopters and non-adopters is becoming a meaningful competitive divide. Practices using automated verification are processing claims faster, collecting more on first submission, and freeing their front desk teams to focus on patient experience and case acceptance. Practices still doing manual verification are spending those same hours on hold with insurance companies. What High-Performing Practices Do Differently Foji.io's analysis identifies the defining operational characteristic of high-performing practices in 2026: they treat insurance verification as a system problem rather than a manual task — using software to handle routine cases autonomously and flagging exceptions for human review. This shift is the single biggest operational differentiator between practices that control their revenue cycle and those that don't. The practical implication: if your front desk team is still spending meaningful time on routine eligibility checks, you haven't solved the problem — you've just hired people to do what software should be doing. Implementing Real-Time Verification: What to Look for in a Solution If you're evaluating automated verification tools for your practice, here's what the 2026 implementation landscape looks like and what capabilities actually matter. PMS Integration: Non-Negotiable Any verification solution worth considering must integrate directly with your practice management system — whether that's Dentrix, Open Dental, Eaglesoft, or another platform. Without native PMS integration, your team is still manually transferring eligibility data between systems, which reintroduces the error risk you're trying to eliminate. PatientDesk's insurance verification and front desk automation features are built with direct PMS integrations across major platforms, ensuring that verified eligibility data flows automatically into patient records without manual data entry. This is the kind of end-to-end integration that actually removes your team from the routine verification loop. Payer Coverage: Breadth Matters As noted earlier, most major clearinghouses connect to 900–1,000 payers — covering the vast majority of commercial plans, Medicare, and Medicaid. When evaluating solutions, ask specifically about coverage for your most common payers and whether the system flags cases that fall outside its automated coverage for manual follow-up. Reporting and Denial Analytics The best verification systems don't just check eligibility — they track outcomes. Look for solutions that report on verification accuracy rates, denial rates tied to eligibility errors, and trends over time. This data is essential for identifying payers or plan types that consistently cause problems and adjusting your workflows accordingly. The Broader Automation Ecosystem Real-time verification is most powerful when it's part of a broader front office automation strategy. PatientDesk AI's dental practice automation platform combines automated insurance verification with AI-powered scheduling, 24/7 phone answering, and patient communication — creating a fully automated front office that handles routine administrative work around the clock without adding headcount. When your front desk team is freed from manual verification, they can redirect that time to higher-value activities: treatment plan follow-up, case acceptance conversations, and patient relationship building. PatientDesk's AI Patient Sales Coordinator is specifically designed to capture that upside — helping practices convert more treatment plans and recover revenue from patients who've gone inactive, using the staff capacity that automation creates. Building Your 2026 Verification Workflow: A Practical Framework Putting this all together, here's what a best-practice real-time verification workflow looks like for a dental practice in 2026: Step 1: Verify at Scheduling (Real-Time Query) The moment a patient books an appointment — whether online, by phone, or in person — your system automatically submits a 270 eligibility query and returns the 271 response within seconds. Your team sees active coverage status, deductible information, remaining benefits, and co-pay requirements before the patient even hangs up the phone. Step 2: Re-Verify 48 Hours Before the Appointment (Batch Query) Your system automatically re-queries all upcoming appointments 48 hours out, catching any coverage changes that occurred since the initial booking. Patients with changed or terminated coverage are flagged for a proactive outreach call — giving your team time to resolve the issue before the appointment, not after. Step 3: Exception Handling Cases that fall outside automated coverage — unusual payers, workers' comp, certain Medicaid managed care plans — are automatically flagged for manual verification with enough lead time to complete the check before the appointment. Step 4: Benefits Communication to Patients Verified benefits information is automatically included in appointment reminders, giving patients a clear picture of their expected out-of-pocket costs before they arrive. This reduces financial surprises at checkout and improves case acceptance for same-day treatment recommendations. Step 5: Denial Tracking and Workflow Improvement Any claim denial tied to an eligibility error is tracked and analyzed to identify patterns — specific payers, plan types, or verification gaps that need workflow adjustments. This continuous improvement loop is what separates practices that maintain 94–96% first-pass acceptance rates from those that plateau at 70–78%. The Bottom Line: Real-Time Verification Is a Revenue Strategy, Not Just an Admin Fix The framing of insurance verification as an "administrative task" is part of what keeps practices stuck in manual workflows. When you look at the full picture — the impact on Days in A/R, first-pass claim acceptance, staff capacity, patient experience, and competitive positioning — real-time automated verification is one of the highest-ROI investments a dental practice can make in 2026. The industry-wide savings opportunity is $711+ million . The per-practice savings are measurable in thousands of dollars per month. The accuracy improvement is 16–26 percentage points. The time savings are 10 to 20 front desk hours per week. The only question is how long your practice can afford to leave that value on the table. If you're ready to move from manual verification to a fully automated eligibility workflow — one that integrates with your PMS, covers 900+ payers, and frees your team to focus on patient care — the technology exists today to make that shift. The practices that make it in 2026 will have a structural revenue cycle advantage that compounds over time. The ones that don't will keep spending their mornings on hold with insurance companies.

title: DeepMind's GNoME Paper Illuminates AI-Driven Materials Discovery, But Challenges Remain
summary: Learn more about how the latest research in AI is impacting materials science.
body_text: The development of new materials is of paramount importance in addressing emerging challenges and meeting evolving needs, such as sustainability concerns and the demand for higher-performance materials. However, the process of developing these new materials is notoriously difficult. It involves balancing a multitude of constraints, such as cost, durability, and specific application requirements, which are often hard to simulate accurately. This complexity is particularly pronounced in high-stakes industries where the margin for error is minimal, making traditional methods of materials discovery—largely based on trial and error and extensive physical testing—both time-consuming and inefficient. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool to assist in scientific fields, such as drug discovery . However, AI was not much used in the materials discovery process. At Osium AI, we noticed this gap and therefore built our technology with the strong belief that AI can drive valuable insights, significantly accelerating the pace of materials innovation . Our conviction is that AI can not only enhance the ability to discover new materials but also help optimize the development processes, reducing both time and cost. At Osium AI, we developed our proprietary AI-powered platform to accelerate materials development well before Google DeepMind’s release of the Graph Networks for Materials Exploration (GNoME) paper a few months ago. We were excited to see this paper highlight the benefits of AI for materials discovery, in alignment with our belief in its transformative potential and paving the way for further innovation in the field. The release of the GNoME paper has sparked widespread discussions in the materials science field, making it natural for us to cover their research, highlight their achievements, and assess how the paper positions itself within the broader materials science industry. Despite its strong potential, GNoME approach lacks industrial proximity , not taking into account industrial constraints. This is where Osium AI comes into play, bridging the gap between theoretical research and practical industrial applications .

Resideo Redefines Smart Comfort with Launch of Honeywell Home X8S Smart Thermostat Delivers Precision Comfort Control and Seamless Integration with Ring Video Doorbells Company News 12/03/25 SCOTTSDALE, Ariz., Dec. 03, 2025 – Resideo Technologies (NYSE: REZI) , a leading global provider of solutions for home comfort, security and safety, today launched a new style of smart comfort: the Honeywell Home X8S smart thermostat. From America’s No. 1 most trusted thermostat brand, 1 the Honeywell Home X8S smart thermostat conveniently streams live video from compatible doorbells on the largest touchscreen in its class. It offers a combination of precision sensing and control, intuitive touchscreen interface and premium design, delivering the brand’s smartest thermostat yet. “Smart comfort is more than just the perfect temperature – it's understanding and actively managing your air quality, knowing that you won’t have a surprise HVAC system failure, and seamlessly saving money and energy,” said Pat Tessier, Vice President of Product Development for Honeywell Home and First Alert solutions at Resideo. “The X8S does all that you would expect of a premium thermostat, and so much more – like seeing who’s at the door without lifting a finger through our doorbell integration. It’s the centerpiece of a smarter, simplified home.” New Honeywell Home X8S Smart Thermostat Features Backed by over a century of innovation, the Honeywell Home X8S smart thermostat is ideal for customers seeking a sleek, modern design and a smarter, energy-efficient solution. Its key benefits and features include: Convenient video doorbell streaming and intercom : With a first-of-its-kind video doorbell integration, 2 homeowners can view live video streams from First Alert® or Ring® doorbells and speak to visitors directly from the thermostat. Intuitive customizable touchscreen : The sleek, five-inch touchscreen enables intuitive operation of temperature programming and customized idle screens that display information the homeowner wants to see, including a five-day weather forecast, digital clocks, indoor air quality (IAQ) information, design themes and color combinations to match any home décor. Awareness and control of IAQ : In addition to maintaining ideal temperature, the smart thermostat monitors humidity, tracks volatile organic compounds and estimates carbon dioxide levels. HVAC installers can help homeowners maintain optimal IAQ with humidity and ventilation control to keep the home’s air fresh. 3 Proactive HVAC system performance alerts : The X8S smart thermostat continuously monitors the HVAC system, and a notification is sent to both the homeowner and their technician 4 when an unusual pattern is detected – enabling a proactive service that helps prevent minor issues from escalating into costly system failures or unexpected loss of comfort. Intelligent energy savings : The thermostat’s optional Smart Room Sensors help prioritize room comfort when at home, Adaptive Recovery technology learns how long the heating and cooling system takes to reach the programmed temperature, and auto-away technologies on the First Alert® app adjust the system automatically to deliver energy savings when away. Honeywell Home smart thermostat users save on average $204 annually when using its recommended scheduling feature consistently. 5 Compatibility and Smart Home Integration The Honeywell Home X8S smart thermostat, available in bold black or classic white models, supports a wide range of HVAC system configurations and has dual-band WiFi compatibility. It is built on the familiar Honeywell Home UWP® wall-mounting plate for easy installation. Homeowners can manage set points and schedules on the thermostat or the First Alert app. The X8S smart thermostat is Matter certified and compatible with Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant and Apple Home for easy voice control. Pricing and Purchase The Honeywell Home X8S smart thermostat is available on HoneywellHome.com and at U.S. and Canadian retailers for $219.99 (U.S. MSRP). Nearly half of consumers 6 prefer that a professional install their thermostat, and Resideo's independent HVAC professionals can install a variety of trusted Honeywell Home smart thermostats with enhanced IAQ and diagnostic features.
